extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (ethics), scholars of Aristotelian thought
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains Aristotle's normative criteria for friendship (Books VIII–IX): types of friendship, their stability, relation to justice/communion, rules of reciprocity, and causes of quarrel. Useful for analyzing or teaching virtue‑ethical accounts of interpersonal relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship chosen for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship is choiceworthy in itself — men delight in friendship for its own sake rather than for incidental benefits like honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle contrasts delight in being the object of friendship (honour) with delight in entertaining the sentiment: true friendship is the latter. Example: people who love their friends find pleasure in the feeling itself; mothers who care for adopted children without expecting return illustrate this. Anti‑pattern: seeking friendship primarily as a route to honour or future advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship consists in feeling, not merely being the object
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship 'is thought to consist in feeling, rather than being the object of, the sentiment of Friendship'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by examples where one party cares without reciprocation (mothers giving children away but still bearing affection). Emphasizes active benevolent attitude rather than passive reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence of friends = proportionate affectionate feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The excellence (virtue) of friends is to entertain the sentiment in due proportion; where this exists friendships are stable and permanent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friends who are 'fond of their friends' and exercise this sentiment appropriately are praised and form lasting bonds. Implies moderation and right degree of concern as a criterion of good friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of goodness fosters stable friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality and similarity, especially similarity of goodness, tie friends together: good men are stable in themselves and towards others and thus form lasting friendships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good persons neither ask nor render degrading services; they prevent wrongdoing. Thus moral similarity yields durable friendship; anti‑pattern: friends united by vice lack stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendships of profit/pleasure are conditional and unstable
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship based on profit or pleasure is short‑lived and depends on mutual benefit or amusement; it endures only while the utility/pleasure continues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: people connected by profit (poor with rich) or pleasure (bacchanals, club‑fellows). These friendships dissolve when the shared advantage/pleasure ceases; they are the likeliest sites of fault‑finding and quarrel.

rubrics_metrics.name: The three kinds of friendship: goodness, pleasure, utility
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three kinds of friendship — based on goodness (virtue), pleasure, and advantage (utility) — each with distinct motives and stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendship based on goodness is disinterested and permanent; pleasure friendships depend on shared enjoyment; utility friendships depend on mutual advantage and are vulnerable to complaint and breaking when motives cease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship co‑extensive with communion and justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship and justice have the same object‑matter and are co‑extensive with forms of communion: the extent and kind of friendship correspond to the degree of communal sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains proverb 'the goods of friends are common'. Different friendships (brothers, companions, fellow‑citizens) imply different principles of justice and differing extents of sharing; acts done to friends are intensified in wrongfulness (e.g., worse to rob a companion than a fellow‑citizen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of interpersonal relation should match principle of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of justice (and thus friendship) varies by relationship: paternal rule resembles kingship, husband‑wife resembles aristocracy, brothers resemble timocracy/democracy, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use proportionality appropriate to the relation: parents have paternal claims, husband rules where right, brothers are equal in many respects. Anti‑pattern: applying one domestic rule (e.g., despotism) where a different, more appropriate rule should govern.

rubrics_metrics.name: No friendship where there is no commonality (inanimate tools, slaves qua slaves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship requires something in common (share in law/agreements); there is no friendship toward inanimate things or toward a slave qua slave because there is nothing in common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A slave qua man may be the object of some friendship, but qua slave (an animate tool) there is no friendship. This sets a boundary condition for when friendship is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communion (shared life/work) as basis of friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: All instances of friendship are based upon some form of communion — shared activity, community, or joint pursuit of advantage, pleasure, or life in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include crew of a vessel, comrades in war, members of a tribe, religious assemblies. The greater and more life‑long the communion (e.g., the political/social communion), the broader the friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity and proportion in unequal friendships
rubrics_metrics.description: In friendships where parties are unequal, friendship should be rendered in proportion to the superiority of one party; proportionate reciprocity equalises and preserves friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one party advantages another in money or goodness, the other should repay with what is appropriate to his power (honour, profit). Friendship requires what is possible rather than a strict mathematical equivalence; examples include obligations to parents and gods where exact repayment is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different forms of requital: measure by receiver's advantage vs doer's intention
rubrics_metrics.description: Dispute whether kindness should be measured by the good done to the receiver (standard of utility) or by the kind intention of the doer (standard of virtue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle suggests: in utility friendships the advantage to the receiver is the appropriate standard; in friendships based on goodness the motive/intention of the doer is the proper standard. Example: beneficiaries may depreciate a gift as small for giver, while giver claims it was the best he had.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal vs moral kinds of utility‑based friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship-for-advantage divides into a 'legal' (stipulated, quid pro quo) and a 'moral' (unspecified credit) kind; legal obligations admit no dispute but moral ones create expectations and potential complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the legal kind obligations are specified (tradesmanlike or by agreement) and sometimes not actionable at law (credit arrangements); in the moral kind a man gives as to a friend but expects equivalent in spirit, leading to quarrels if expectations differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fault‑finding most likely in utility friendships
rubrics_metrics.description: Fault‑finding and blame arise chiefly in friendships motivated by utility because requirements continually enlarge and one party feels shortchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure‑based friendships generate fewer quarrels (one may simply cease association), and goodness‑based friendships avoid such contention because both parties share the end of doing kindness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties must clarify the rate or understanding of exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: When mutual services/benefits are not self‑evidently equivalent (especially in love or mixed motives), quarrels arise over who fixes the rate — the giver or the receiver — so parties should fix the understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protagoras' example: teacher allowed learner to estimate worth. Rule sometimes adopted: 'With specified reward a friend should be content.' Anti‑pattern: taking money in advance and failing to perform (criticised).

rubrics_metrics.name: Different expectations for relationships of origin and upbringing
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships stemming from kinship and common upbringing (parents, siblings, cousins) are stronger due to shared origin, longer time, and greater opportunities to prove loyalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parents love offspring as part of themselves; time and early attachment make parental love stronger. Brothers' similarity of age/upbringing parallels companions. Strength of kinship bond varies by distance from the common ancestor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation asymmetry: children as perpetual debtors to parents
rubrics_metrics.description: Children owe more and can never fully requite parents for benefits of being, maintenance, and education; thus sons are always debtors and ought not to disown fathers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although theoretically fathers can cast off sons (those to whom anything is owed may cast off debtors), natural friendship and human nature make such severance rare except in extreme depravity. Implies a normative rule about enduring filial obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teachers/learners and non‑market goods: requital by intention and ability
rubrics_metrics.description: For goods without a money‑measure (e.g., philosophical teaching), value cannot be properly priced; requital should be 'to do what one can', comparable to obligations to gods or parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical teaching is not measurably equivalent; the appropriate standard of requital is intention and doing one’s best within ability rather than precise exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quarrels arise from mismatched motives and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Quarrels occur when parties have different motives (pleasure vs utility vs virtue) or expect different results; failing to attain one's specific object is tantamount to getting nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: musician who promised on differing assumptions; parties must align on whether interaction is for pleasure or gain to avoid dispute. Ensuring common understanding of the relationship’s motive reduces conflict.
